New York City has an empty storefront problem.
According to a new City Comptroller’s Office report, 1 in 9 storefronts citywide was vacant as of September, with Manhattan and Brooklyn exceeding the citywide average. The city has launched a dashboard to track street-level vacancies.
“Thriving commercial corridors are essential to the health of New York City’s economy and neighborhoods,” City Comptroller Mark Levine said. “In many ways, New York City has recovered since the pandemic, but the comeback has been uneven, with storefronts sitting empty in many communities that deserve bustling activity.”
Last summer, between July and September, nearly 142,000 storefronts were shuttered, according to the findings. The number represented a slight increase from the previous quarter, and was above pre-pandemic levels. Since summer 2023, the citywide storefront vacancy rate has remained above 11%.
Across the five boroughs, Manhattan had the highest vacancy rate at just over 13%. Brooklyn was the second-highest at about 12.7%. Queens’ vacancy rate was nearly 10%, but the borough had the largest quarterly increase in shuttered retail spaces. The vacancy rate was 8% on Staten Island and slightly higher in the Bronx.
But city neighborhoods including the Financial District, Tribeca, Ocean Hill, East New York and Old Astoria-Hallets Point have some of the highest vacancy rates, all around 20%. Overall, the city recorded a net loss of more than 200 small businesses between spring and summer of this year, the report said.
The dashboard comes at a busy period for businesses and shoppers alike. According to the New York City Economic Development Corporation, city businesses experience a 35% boost in customer traffic during the period from Black Friday through December, generating about $500 million in sales.
Levine said the goal of the storefront vacancy dashboard is to assist policymakers, small businesses and community organizations track the economic status of shopping districts across the five boroughs. The dashboard will be updated quarterly.
“Keeping an up-to-date accounting of the severity of this problem is essential for us in government to develop solutions,” Levine said.

The Ramapough Lenape Nation, one of New Jersey's few remaining Native American tribes, has joined the opposition in one of the state’s most contentious housing battles, challenging a wealthy developer's plan to build nearly 500 apartments on a wooded mountain in West Orange.
Last year, the town’s planning board rejected a proposal by billionaire real estate developers, the Wilf family, ruling the plan environmentally unsound and raising transportation concerns.
The development would require clearing hundreds of mature trees. The Wilfs, whose patriarch, Zygi Wilf, owns the Minnesota Vikings, have appealed the decision and are asking Essex County Superior Court to overturn the denial.
Opponents of the project have vowed to keep fighting. Now, members of the Ramapough Lenape are joining their ranks, arguing that the property contains sacred artifacts left by their ancestors thousands of years ago.
At a January 2026 planning board hearing, Chief Vincent Mann of the Ramapough Lenape Nation testified that more than 100 ceremonial stone markers — intentionally arranged spiritual rock formations that acted as prayer structures — are scattered throughout the forest.
“Many, many years ago, before first contact, our ancestors are the ones that actually placed them there. They placed them in a prayerful way,” he said.
Sandy Crisafulli, a representative for the Wilfs, declined to respond to questions about whether the family knew of the artifacts or how it plans to address the tribe’s claims. Their attorneys have argued to Judge Aldo Russo that the Ramapough Lenape should not be allowed to intervene because the planning board did not address the tribe’s concerns when it rejected the project.
The Wilf family has owned the Essex County property, located on the second ridge of the Watchung Mountains, for decades. The ancient, volcanically formed ridge is composed of bedrock millions of years old. The forest represents one of the last vestiges of the Ramapough Lenape’s ancestral homeland. Twenty years ago, the same planning board rejected the family’s proposal to build 136 single-family homes there.
The prospect of development resurfaced in 2020, when a proposal for the apartment complex — which includes more than 100 units for low- and moderate-income families — was incorporated into West Orange’s affordable housing plan. Under a 50-year-old state statute, every municipality in New Jersey must develop a set number of affordable units. After roughly 30 planning board hearings over several years, the proposal ultimately failed in May 2026, when the board deadlocked 4-4.
The Ramapough Lenape trace their roots to northern New Jersey’s Highlands, thousands of years before Dutch and English settlers arrived. Bruce Afran, an attorney representing the tribe, said Indigenous communities lost the land in the 1600s through a series of treaties imposed by the British.
“There was an inherently unfair bargain in which these lands were lost through treaties that only the British could read and understand,” Afran said. “So by any stretch of reasoning, the lands really were stolen.”
In his planning board testimony, Mann described not only the stone markers but also three serpent walls — stacked stone formations that wind across the landscape in a snake-like fashion, like a swimming water serpent — and a directional tree, which was intentionally bent as a sapling to grow in a way that marks the route to a path, a sacred area or a water source.
“We're sitting on the precipice of ruining forever the prayers of our ancestors that were placed in a particular way,” Mann testified.
Mann, who lives in Andover, about 35 miles northeast of the West Orange property, declined to be interviewed.
In court filings, the Ramapough Lenape have also argued that the artifacts fall under protections in New Jersey’s State Development and Redevelopment Plan. Afran acknowledged that those protections do not, by themselves, prohibit development.
“Like everything in law, it does get a little more complicated,” he said. “The state plan says these have to be taken into account in zoning, planning, and development decisions. It doesn't in itself bar development.”
Afran said he expects the judge to decide on Dec. 4 whether the tribe can join the lawsuit.

He is also the author of the book, “The Secret Files: Bill De Blasio, The NYPD, and the Broken Promises of Police Reform.” In 2019, he was a finalist for the Livingston Award for Young Journalists. Mayor Zohran Mamdani is recovering in Gracie Mansion after successfully undergoing surgery on Friday to repair an Achilles tendon injured on the soccer pitch last week, City Hall spokesperson said.
The procedure began at 11:33 a.m. and ended at 12:42 p.m., mayor’s spokesperson Joe Calvello said in a statement posted on social media. The statement did not disclose where the procedure was performed.
“The surgery was successful, and the mayor is expected to make a full recovery,” Calvello said in the statement. “He was discharged from the hospital and is now resting comfortably at Gracie Mansion.”
He added, “We are extremely grateful for the first-class care the mayor received from the medical staff today.”
Mamdani, 35, sustained the non-contact injury in a soccer match last week between City Hall staffers and members of the media. The injury is expected to limit the mayor's movement for months to come.
Mamdani arrived late to the Nov. 19 game at an indoor soccer field in the Financial District. He later told reporters he didn’t stretch before playing.
“I forgot that I was 35,” he said.
He said ahead of the procedure he expected to wear a protective boot for six to eight weeks and won’t be able to play soccer again for nine months.
First Deputy Mayor Dean Fuleihan is leading day-to-day operations today, Calvello said.

State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, a Yonkers Democrat who made history as the first Black woman to lead a legislative conference in Albany, died unexpectedly on Friday. She was 76.
Stewart-Cousins’ longtime spokesperson, Mike Murphy, confirmed her death. The cause was not immediately disclosed.
Her passing comes less than two weeks after Senate Democrats voted to give her another two-year term as majority leader, one of the three most powerful positions in New York state government.
The news sent shockwaves through the state Capitol, where Stewart-Cousins was a towering figure who played an outsize role in all substantial legislation that has passed since Democrats took control of the Senate in 2018.
“Andrea was more than just a remarkable public servant,” said Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins, a longtime Stewart-Cousins ally. “She was a trailblazer, a dedicated advocate for the people of our county, and a leader whose impact will continue to be felt for generations.”
Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, left, and Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie, right, hold a joint news conference with Democratic lawmakers to call on Congress to prevent Medicaid cuts in a final spending bill on June 9, 2025, at the Capitol in Albany.
Will Waldron/Albany Times Union via Getty Images
The Yonkers Police Department said in a statement Friday evening it received a call requesting a welfare check at Stewart-Cousins' Yonkers residence at about 12:10 p.m. The caller identified themselves as a relative of the senator and reported that there was no answer at the door or by telephone.
Responding officers made entry into the residence and found Stewart-Cousins unresponsive in her bed. First responders immediately rendered aid and attempted lifesaving measures, to no avail. She was pronounced deceased a short while later by EMS personnel, the statement said.
Members of the Yonkers Police Department Detective Division responded to the scene and conducted an initial investigation. Following an examination and consultation with the senator’s physician, investigators concluded there were no signs of foul play or unusual circumstances, according to the statement.
First elected to the Senate in 2006, Stewart-Cousins steadily rose through the ranks before her Democratic colleagues elected her minority leader in 2012.
Over time, she steadied what had been a tumultuous conference rocked by infighting and scandal. Under her watch, Democrats won enough seats over several election cycles to retake the Senate majority in 2018, knocking Republicans from the majority perch they had held for the better part of a century and making Stewart-Cousins the first woman to lead the Senate.
Since then, Stewart-Cousins was one of three people — along with the governor and Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie — to negotiate state budgets and major pieces of legislation. As leader, she helped pass bills to strengthen state abortion protections and reform the criminal-justice system, including a dramatic reduction in the number of crimes subject to cash bail.
Senate Democratic Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, center, joins a group of prominent women leaders to demand support for legislation allowing cities and counties to raise wages above the state's minimum wage on April 30, 2014, during a demonstration at the Capitol in Albany.
John Carl D'Annibale /Albany Times Union via Getty Images
Stewart-Cousins’ tenure as majority leader bridged the terms of Gov. Kathy Hochul and former Gov. Andrew Cuomo, both of whom expressed shock at the news of her death.
“New York is a better place because of her. And I am a better person for having known her,” Hochul said in a statement. “I will miss Andrea dearly.”
Cuomo called Stewart-Cousins a “trailblazer.”
“As the first woman and first Black woman to lead a legislative majority in New York state, she made history,” Cuomo said in a statement. “She stood up for her members and fought for what she believed was right, without hesitation and always with dignity, grace and class."
Tributes flowed in from elsewhere.
“A true trailblazer and a tireless champion for working families, Andrea made history as the first woman to lead a legislative chamber in New York State,” New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, a Democrat, posted on social media. “She devoted her life to public service, lifting up others and opening doors for generations of New Yorkers to follow.”
Assemblymember Emily Gallagher, a Democrat who represents parts of Brooklyn, said, “Andrea wasn’t just a great politician, she was a leader who took her role fighting for a better world seriously. She was a thoughtful, kind and steady force in Albany and a mentor to so many women.”
Speaker Heastie also hailed Stewart-Cousins as “a trailblazer – the first woman and the first Black woman to hold the gavel as majority leader in the Senate.”
But he added that her reach extended further.
“She was a fighter for the rights of all New Yorkers,” Heastie said. “I called her my Wonder Twin because it was a pleasure and an honor to stand beside her as our houses enacted the groundbreaking and progressive legislation we have long fought for.”

Weather for the rest of the holiday weekend and Saturday’s postponed Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will be a breeze compared to Thursday’s mayhem.
The National Weather Service is predicting mild weather for the rest of Friday, with temperatures in the 50s, partly cloudy skies, brief passing showers in the afternoon or evening, and wind gusts up to 35 mph.
Clear and dry weather is expected on Saturday, with sustained winds reaching up to 15 mph and gusts up to 25 mph, according to the weather service, below the threshold that parade requires to proceed with its iconic giant balloons.
“Conditions are much better for a parade on Saturday,” said National Weather Service meteorologist David Stark. “The winds won't be anywhere near as strong.”
The weather was a different story on Thursday, when heavy rains caused flooding in coastal and low-lying areas, and strong winds downed trees and power lines.
Central Park recorded 2.18 inches of rain, topping the previous record of 1.91 inches for Nov. 26, set in 1996, according to the weather service. The Rockaways remained under a flood advisory into Friday morning.
More than 100,000 homes in the Garden State were still without power early Friday, down from 179,000 on Thanksgiving Day.
More than 15,000 Con Ed customers in New York lost power during the nor'easter, according to Con Ed. In Westchester County, more than 9,000 households lost power, and many still were still waiting for service to be restored.
On Long Island, at the height of the storm, more than 40,000 homes lost power and the total was 11,000 in Orange and Rockland. Only a few thousand customers were still without service Friday, according to the utility officials.
Only general flight delays were reported at the region's airports.

Advocates' vision for discounted NJ Transit fares could be an uphill climb
By

Jasai Howard-Wright has always relied on public transit to get around.
The Seton Hall University student lives on campus in South Orange without a car. So running errands, meeting friends or getting to activities outside the Essex County campus means hopping on an NJ Transit bus or train. It’s something he’s used to. Howard-Wright said he grew up in Somerville without a car, so taking the bus around the Central Jersey suburbs of Somerset County was a way of life.
But the bus isn’t free, and a cash-strapped college student can feel the costs add up quickly. Howard-Wright estimates at least a quarter of his expenses are transit-related.
“A lot of the money that I earned over the summer is going towards these transportation costs,” Howard-Wright said.
And that cost is constantly rising, with 3% automatic annual fare increases for NJ Transit.
“It used to only cost $10 to get from Somerville to Newark Penn Station. Now it costs almost $15 just to do it. You know, it's crazy,” Howard-Wright said. “It's a $5 increase, and other people might say, ‘Oh, it's only a $5 difference.’ But it adds up these days, especially when everything else is so expensive.”
Howard-Wright is just one of thousands of low-income New Jerseyans transit advocates say should have access to discounted rides on NJ Transit buses, trains and light rail lines.
A coalition of advocacy groups in the Garden State launched the Fair Fares NJ campaign earlier this year. Their goal is to convince state leaders to expand NJ Transit’s reduced fare program to make some people eligible based on income thresholds. It’s currently open to seniors, people with disabilities and military personnel, and offers half-price fares on trains, buses and light rails.
Howard-Wright said a discount would go a long way for him.
“It would just put less stress on our day-to-day lives and help us focus on more essential things such as tuition and, you know, food and stuff like that,” Howard-Wright said.
The campaign is backed by a coalition of more than a dozen transit, environmental and progressive advocacy groups, including the Regional Plan Association, New Jersey Policy Perspective, the New Jersey League of Conservation Voters and the New Jersey Environmental Justice Alliance.
They argue that making transit more accessible would spur other benefits in society.
“Transportation's the game board upon which all other games are played,” said Zoe Baldwin, the vice president of state programs for the Regional Plan Association, which advocates for improving public transit throughout the New York City region. “When you're talking about public health, if you can't reliably access or afford to get to healthcare, that's going to impact public health. It's going to impact unemployment. It's going to impact our traffic. It's going to impact our air quality.”
Many other transit systems around the country already offer reduced fares for low-income riders. New York City’s Fair Fares program offers a 50% discount on subways and eligible buses for people with incomes up to 150% of the federal poverty level. That program will expand to include people making up to 200% of the federal poverty level at the end of November.
More than 370,000 New Yorkers are enrolled in the city’s program, though about 1.3 million will be eligible under its new rules. To try and boost enrollment, the New York City Council passed a law allowing people to simply check a box and enroll in Fair Fares when renewing with SNAP.
Baldwin said the campaign has had talks with NJ Transit and Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s office about expanding New Jersey’s reduced fares program to include income-based eligibility.
NJ Transit President Kris Kolluri said he agrees with the general goal of expanding transit access. But he said if it were to come to fruition, he’d want to see another agency in charge of administering enrollment and handling the fare subsidy because NJ Transit is facing a structural deficit that fluctuates between $100 million and $200 million year-to-year.
“What I would not advise is for someone to impose this laudable goal onto the existing transit balance sheet because that doesn't do anything to help us get out of the hole,” Kolluri said. “But if it serves as a separate program organized by the Legislature, if they think it's the right thing to do, separate and apart from New Jersey Transit, I think it's something I'm sure everybody would be interested in at least hearing about.”
The Fair Fares NJ campaign is not advocating for specific eligibility requirements or administrative structures. Existing programs around the country may serve as models, but NJ Transit is unique as being the only statewide entity of its kind.
“We need to make sure that we're creating a program that works for how the agency works,” Baldwin said.
Alex Ambrose, a senior policy analyst for the New Jersey Policy Perspective think tank, said it's likely the state could tie enrollment in NJ Transit’s reduced fares with enrollment in other programs, like SNAP or utility bill relief efforts.
“There's lots of other programs that people qualify for, and this can be just one more thing we add on top of it,” Ambrose said.
The administration can expand the reduced fare program on its own. But actually funding such a move would likely require help from state lawmakers, either through appropriatio

New York City is taking longer to fix its broken streetlights after last year's nasty winter.
Department of Transportation data shows that city inspectors took more than 10 days in fiscal year 2026 to inspect a quarter of complaints about streetlight outages. During that period from July 2025 to June 2026, there were 36,291 complaints about broken street lights — a 16% increase from the prior fiscal year.
The average number of calendar days for the transportation department to repair a streetlight also increased 60% over that period — from 5.3 calendar days to 8.5 days. The trend was first reported by The City Reporter.
In interviews, some residents of Bay Ridge in Brooklyn said broken streetlights have taken a toll on community safety. Josephine Beckmann, the district manager of Community Board 10, said she is tracking at least seven streetlights that have been out for four months or more, including one near 91st Street and Ridge Boulevard that went dark in October 2025.
"In recent weeks there seem to be many more," she said. "And it feels like it's taking a lot longer for repairs to be made."
The community board currently has 137 complaints about light outages. Fed up with the slow repairs, the board, along with state Sen. Andrew Gounardes and City Councilmember Kayla Santosuosso, wrote a letter to urge the DOT to repair the busted lights in late October.
Jack Ho, a lifelong resident of Bay Ridge, said the lack of light makes it difficult to see on some side streets, making for a treacherous journey.
"You'll randomly come across a bump, and there's no light to help you see it," he said.
Wilson Mejia, 22, said his mother, who is in her 50s, has stopped wanting to leave the house after sundown. "She always says she doesn't really want to go out because it's dark," he said.
Yiana Green said she’s seen raccoons, rats and a skunk on an unlit street.
An analysis by Vital City showed that the top 20 hotspots for recurring complaints about streetlights are concentrated in Queens, Brooklyn, and the Bronx. A single intersection in Ridgewood near Cypress and Myrtle avenues had 14 complaints lodged with 311 since January 2024. A stretch of the Bronx in Norwood drew 40 streetlight complaints, according to the data.
The Department of Transportation aims to inspect a complaint about a streetlight outage within 10 days. But the most recent Mayor's Management Report shows the department met that benchmark only 75% of the time in the most recent fiscal year — down from 94% the year prior.
Transportation department spokesperson Vincent Barone attributed the increase in repair time in part to "the historic winter that brought heavy snowfall, extended freezing temperatures, and more street lighting repairs."
In Crown Heights and Prospect-Lefferts Gardens, another hotspot for streetlight outages, residents say most of the illumination comes from local businesses.
Paco Abraham, 45, a member of local Community Board 9, said a corner of Rogers Avenue was almost entirely dark for most of a year. When a new bodega opened nearby, its signage became the de facto streetlight on the block.
“We shouldn’t be relying on a store to light the street when it’s the responsibility of the city,” he said.
Whether a dark light makes a block more dangerous depends on just how dark it gets and how long it's out for, said Aaron Chalfin, a criminologist at the University of Pennsylvania who has studied lighting and crime in New York and Chicago. In Chicago, a single failed light produced no measurable change in behavior. When two or more lights on a block went out, people stopped walking on it, and crime rose on the lit blocks nearby.
The longer an outage lasts, Chalfin said, the more it affects the community’s overall culture.
"It's a signal that these are not places that are cared for," he said. "These are not places that are prioritized."

It’s the height of high school and middle school application season in New York City. Applications are due Dec. 4 and Dec. 11 respectively.
Students are writing earnest application essays, preparing art portfolios and recording drama audition videos. It’s a complicated, stressful process for both students and parents. Critics say it can worsen existing educational inequities.
The city has the largest school system in the country — and one of the most segregated. The Mamdani administration has come under growing pressure to address racial imbalances across the city’s roughly 1,800 public schools.
Gothamist crunched a wide range of education data, which shows that yawning achievement and opportunity gaps still plague the school system.
Black students have left the city’s schools at disproportionate rates and are far less likely to get an offer from one of the city’s highly competitive specialized high schools. Test scores and graduation rates are significantly lower for Latino and low-income students. And students who are white, Asian and Pacific Islanders or from more affluent families are more likely to be in gifted and talented programs and get into their preferred high schools.
Nicole Brownstein, a spokesperson for New York City Public Schools, said the city will continue investing in standardized, research-backed literacy and math programs to help close these gaps. She pointed to higher test scores for Latino and Black students in eighth grade as signs of progress.
“We know this work has just begun and is far from over,” Brownstein said in an emailed statement.
Here’s Gothamist’s deep dive into the city’s education stats:
Overall enrollment decline
Let’s start with who’s actually in the system.
For close to a decade, the number of students in public schools has been shrinking in the city and across the country, largely the result of low birthrates and more families choosing private schools or homeschooling, according to one study by Brookings.
Here in the five boroughs, enrollment has dropped 9% since 2016, but some students have left the city’s public schools more than others. Black enrollment has plummeted 22% over the past 10 years. White enrollment has only declined by 15% over the same period.
The number of students living in low-income families has also dropped but at a slower pace. They now make up a slightly bigger share of the student population, as rents and other costs have soared and the city has become less affordable. In 2016, those children made up 71% of overall enrollment. Today, that number stands at 73%.
A 2026 study by the advocacy group Available to All found that New York City has the most segregated school system in the United States. Black students are more likely to go to majority Black schools. And the accelerated decline in Black enrollment means those schools are losing the funding that’s tied to enrollment. Less funding means schools are less equipped to support the students who remain.
The drop in students has led to calls for closing some under-enrolled schools. But because low enrollment is more likely at schools in low-income Black and Latino neighborhood, school closures would disproportionately affect those parts of the city.
“Historically there’s been a lot of divestment in Black communities,” said Kathy Hill, an education researcher at NYU. “It affects a lot of institutions, including the schools.”
3-K and pre-K enrollment
While overall enrollment has shrunk, the number of the city’s youngest learners has continued to grow. Enrollment in 3-K has increased since the program launched as a pilot in fall 2017 and has since expanded to every school district in the city. The number of students in 3-K is 13% higher this year compared to 2021, even as Pre-K enrollment for 4-year-olds has shrunk slightly over the same period.
Neither program is compulsory in New York. But education research shows that early childhood education programs can significantly boost cognitive development and academic achievement. One 2020 study found that students living in poverty can especially benefit.
But not all groups are signing up at the same rate. While Pre-K enrollment has increased among Asian and Pacific Islander, Latino, white and economically disadvantaged families, according to city data, fewer Black students are now enrolled in pre-K compared to five years ago.
Halley Potter, an education advocate and a former policy director at the Century Foundation, said that decrease is likely due to the disproportionate decline in Black student enrollment overall.
“A lot of it has to do with Black families moving out of the city because it’s unaffordable,” Potter said. “It might also intersect with the exodus of families with young children.”
In an effort to address inequities in early childhood education, the Mamdani administration earlier this year doubled the initial expansion plan of 3-K, adding 2,000 more seats.
Standardized test scores
Students in grades three through eight are required to take standardized tests each year in math, English language arts and science. Test scores have long fluctuated, but the data shows a persistent gap between white and Asian and Pacific Islander students on one side, and Black and Latino students on the other.
